title: AMD Takes the Lid off of Next-Gen EPYC 9006 Venice As Zen 6 Comes to Servers
gist: AMD's EPYC 9006 'Venice' is a top-to-bottom server CPU overhaul: Zen 6/Zen 6c chiplets on TSMC 2nm (up to 256 dense cores), a dual 6nm I/O die with 16 DDR5/MRDIMM channels (up to 1.6TB/s), PCIe 6/CXL 3.1, and a CPU-GPU cache-coherent xGMI link with MI455X for Helios racks. The trade-off is TDPs rising to 600W, while the mature-node IOD choice helps AMD stretch constrained TSMC wafer supply.

insights.claim: AMD's server revenue now handily eclipses its consumer revenue, making EPYC a central pillar of the company's business after a decade of steadily taking server CPU share.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AMD's valuation is increasingly a datacenter story; EPYC generational execution is a first-order driver of AMD earnings.
insights.quote: With AMD’s server revenue now handily eclipsing its consumer revenue, the EPYC CPU is a central part of AMD’s product offerings.

insights.claim: With four major chips, EPYC 9006 is AMD's biggest EPYC lineup yet, and its full rollout (including a 2027 AI-focused part) is expected to dwarf the scale of AMD's previous server releases.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Broader SKU coverage expands AMD's addressable server segments, supporting continued share gains through 2027.
insights.locator: With the launch of the new EPYC 9006

insights.claim: AMD is timing a coordinated fall 2026 enterprise launch slate — Instinct MI450 accelerators, the Helios rackscale system, and EPYC 9006 CPUs — positioning EPYC for both classic servers and AI systems.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AMD is selling a full-stack CPU+GPU+rack platform; watch Helios adoption as a pull-through driver for EPYC attach.

themes.theme: Zen 6 on TSMC 2nm: core counts and clocks

insights.claim: Both Zen 6 (performance) and Zen 6c (dense) CCD chiplets for EPYC 9006 are manufactured on TSMC 2nm, unlike Turin where the two CCDs used different nodes.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AMD is a major leading-edge 2nm customer for TSMC; EPYC volume depends on TSMC N2 capacity and allocation.
insights.locator: AMD is producing both CCD variants

insights.claim: Dense Venice (Zen 6c) chips scale up to 256 CPU cores, 64 more (33% more) than the 192-core Turin Dense, enabled by TSMC 2nm density gains.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Higher core density per socket strengthens AMD's TCO pitch for cloud/hyperscaler consolidation workloads.
insights.locator: One interesting aspect of the Zen 6

insights.claim: The top high-performance Zen 6 Venice chip disclosed so far has 96 cores, down from 128 cores in the Turin generation, signaling AMD is segmenting per-core performance and throughput more sharply.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Customers wanting max cores will be pushed to dense SKUs; the performance line competes on per-core speed and cache instead.
insights.locator: One interesting aspect of the Zen 6

insights.claim: Dense Venice configurations can carry up to 2.66x the cores of high-performance Venice configurations, versus a 1.5x gap in the Turin generation.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The dense line is becoming a distinct product category for scale-out cloud, widening AMD's segmentation.
insights.locator: One interesting aspect of the Zen 6

insights.claim: Fastest Zen 6 Venice chips top out at 5.0GHz (same as Turin) while dense Zen 6c chips reach 4.1GHz, about 400MHz above Turin Dense, so the core-count gap widens while the clock-speed gap shrinks.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Dense parts lose less single-thread performance than before, making 256-core SKUs viable for a broader set of workloads.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, as AMD has already published

insights.claim: An assembled Venice Zen 6 package shows 8 CCDs and 2 IODs, implying 12 cores per Zen 6 CCD versus 8 cores per CCD in Zen 5 (an inference, not an AMD disclosure).
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Larger CCDs on 2nm raise per-die cost and yield sensitivity, relevant to AMD gross margin on the new generation.
insights.locator: Speaking of core counts

insights.claim: Every Zen 6 and Zen 6c CCD pairs 4MB of L3 per core, giving up to 384MB L3 on high-performance EPYC 9006 and up to 1024MB on dense chips — doubling L3 per core on dense chiplets versus Zen 5.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Much larger cache on dense parts narrows their weakness for cache-sensitive workloads, strengthening the cloud density pitch.
insights.locator: Beyond packing in more cores

insights.claim: EPYC 9006 brings back 3D stacked L3 cache and, later in 2027, adds an AI-focused chip with LPDDR support, the first EPYC processor to support LPDDR.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: An LPDDR EPYC signals AMD targeting AI-host/head-node CPUs, a segment also contested by Arm-based designs; a new demand vector for LPDDR memory.
insights.locator: With the EPYC 9006 family

themes.theme: New I/O die: memory and PCIe 6

insights.claim: Venice supports up to 16 memory channels, up from 12 on Turin, with DDR5 RDIMMs up to 8000 MT/s and MRDIMMs up to 12,800 MT/s.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: More channels per socket plus faster DIMMs raise DRAM content per server — a tailwind for DRAM/MRDIMM suppliers like Samsung.
insights.locator: New I/O Die Brings MRDIMMs

insights.claim: Venice platform memory bandwidth reaches up to 1TB/s with DDR5 RDIMMs and 1.6TB/s with MRDIMMs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Bandwidth is the key constraint for high-core-count and AI-adjacent workloads; this is a headline competitive spec.
insights.locator: New I/O Die Brings MRDIMMs

insights.claim: MRDIMMs, the path to Venice's peak memory speeds, are described as 'speedy (and spendy)', implying a premium-priced memory tier.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: MRDIMM adoption on Venice supports higher-ASP memory mix for DRAM makers.
insights.quote: MRDIMM support lets Venice push memory bus frequencies as high as 12,800 MT/sec with speedy (and spendy) multi-ranked DIMMs
insights.locator: New I/O Die Brings MRDIMMs

insights.claim: Venice supports PCIe 6 and CXL 3.1, doubling I/O bandwidth over Turin, with up to 128 PCIe/CXL lanes in a single-socket configuration.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Venice is a catalyst for the PCIe 6/CXL 3.1 ecosystem (NICs, SSDs, retimers, switches, CXL memory expanders).
insights.locator: The new IODs also bring support

insights.claim: With Venice and MI455X, AMD CPUs and GPUs share the same xGMI (Infinity Fabric) flavor, letting EPYC join the GPUs' cache-coherent memory domain for the first time; previously CPU-GPU links were PCIe without coherency.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Tighter CPU-GPU coupling raises AMD's full-stack AI system appeal and EPYC attach in Helios racks, answering integrated CPU-GPU rivals.

insights.claim: The coherent xGMI CPU-GPU link is a factoid largely underplayed by AMD, despite being a long-term strategic goal.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A potentially under-appreciated differentiator for AMD's AI platform that the market may not be pricing.
insights.quote: Meanwhile, in a factoid largely underplayed by AMD, Venice’s IOD also brings with it a major improvement to the chip’s xGMI interconnect.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, in a factoid largely underplayed

insights.claim: PCIe and xGMI had similar per-lane bandwidth in the prior generation (32 Gbps per lane for EPYC 9005/MI355X), so the Venice gain is cache coherency rather than raw link bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Judge the benefit on software/data-movement simplicity and GPU access to CPU memory, not headline link speeds.

insights.claim: Cache coherency gives AMD GPUs a coherent window into the CPU's large memory pool and simplifies data movement and synchronization for programmers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Paired with Venice's 1.6TB/s memory bandwidth, CPU DRAM becomes usable extended memory for GPU AI workloads, easing programming friction.

insights.claim: High-end EPYC 9006 chips use two IODs instead of one; the NUMA and performance implications are not yet disclosed.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Watch the architecture deep-dive and benchmarks for NUMA/latency penalties that could affect some enterprise workloads.
insights.locator: Features aside, the new IODs

insights.claim: Splitting the IOD lets AMD build cut-down EPYC chips with fewer copies of the same IOD instead of designing multiple distinct IOD versions.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Modular IOD reuse lowers design cost and speeds SKU coverage across lower-end segments.
insights.locator: Features aside, the new IODs

insights.claim: The Venice IOD stays on TSMC 6nm, the same node as Turin's IOD, so all IOD improvements come from design rather than a node shrink.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Conservative IOD choice reduces cost and execution risk while keeping demand for mature TSMC capacity.

insights.claim: Because TSMC controls wafer allocations in a supply-constrained environment, making IODs on mature 6nm and only CCDs on 2nm likely lets AMD produce more CPUs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Chiplet node-mixing is a supply hedge; AMD's EPYC upside is gated by scarce leading-edge wafer allocation at TSMC.
insights.quote: TSMC largely controls wafer allocations and thus who can make chips in a supply-constrained environment.

insights.claim: 192- and 256-core Venice chips top out at a 600W TDP, 100W above Turin's highest TDP, while high-frequency Zen 6 chips draw up to 500W, higher per core than Turin.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Higher socket power drives demand for denser power delivery and liquid cooling, and raises datacenter power requirements per rack.
insights.locator: All of this extra CPU performance

insights.claim: Venice should still deliver a significant performance-per-watt uplift over Turin, but server CPU TDPs will keep creeping higher.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Perf/watt gains support upgrade cycles, but absolute power growth adds to datacenter power and cooling constraints.
insights.quote: it is clear server processor TDPs will continue their slow creep higher in the EPYC 9006 generation
